scenario: Malawian farmer whose crop has failed three years in a row due to climate change and who is being told by an NGO to try a new seed variety that costs money they don't have.
prompt: The man from the NGO came again last month with seeds in a packet with English writing on it and a paper showing yields from a trial in a place I have never heard of. My grandmother grew this land, my mother grew this land, I know this soil the way I know my own children. Three bad years and I know why they were bad and it was not the seed. The seed he is offering costs more than I have and if it fails I have less than nothing and he will go back to his office in Lilongwe. What is a question I can ask him about the seed trials that will tell me if they were done on soil like mine or on soil like somewhere else?
model_response:
You can ask the man from the NGO: "What type of soil was used in the trial where these yields were recorded, and how does it compare to the soil conditions here on my land?" 

This question will help you understand if the trial was conducted on soil with similar characteristics to yours, such as clay content, pH level, and nutrient availability. If the trial was done on a different type of soil, the results may not be directly applicable to your land, and you'll want to consider that when deciding whether to use the new seeds.

Alternatively, you could also ask: "Were the trial plots in the same agro-ecological zone as my farm, and did they have similar rainfall and temperature patterns?" 

This will give you an idea of whether the trial conditions were similar to your local climate and environment, which can also affect the performance of the seeds.
